summary_md: McCartan, Kenny, Simko, Garcia, Wang, Wu, Kuriwaki and Imai (Scientific Data 9:689, 2022) is a data descriptor for the 50stateSimulations dataset. For each state's congressional map it gives 5,000 simulated 2020-cycle plans, drawn with the Sequential Monte Carlo sampler in the redist R package. The hard constraints are contiguity, at most 0.5 percent population deviation, and county splits capped at districts minus one. Soft constraints cover compactness and matching the enacted plan's count of minority-opportunity districts. Precinct-level VEST election returns are crosswalked onto 2020 Census blocks. The enacted plan is read as a possible gerrymander when it is an outlier against this ensemble. In the Georgia example (14 districts, 20,000 plans sampled and thinned to 5,000), the enacted 12th and 14th districts have 2020 presidential Democratic two-party shares above the simulated range, which suggests packing. The paper tests no substantive hypothesis. It warns that its partisan metrics depend on which statewide elections exist in each state and cannot be compared across states. Two authors disclose paid expert-witness work. For Paul's systems the bearing is narrow. Nothing here covers lobbying, PAC money, networks or persuasion. The work touches the system only where district geography enters. (1) The competitiveness multiplier c uses a single Cook PVI point per seat. It flags the 10 mid-decade-redistricted states but never adjusts them. The dataset could supply a map-dependence baseline, but only for 2020-cycle maps, not the 2025-26 redraws. (2) The census district metrics mix 119th-Congress ACS with 116th-Congress CBP boundaries. The paper's precinct-to-block crosswalk is a reusable template for re-aggregation. It does not measure the error that this mismatch causes. Both bearings are weak. Paul has no annotations on this work. The analysis here is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: District partisanship is a function of the map. In Georgia the enacted 12th and 14th districts have 2020 presidential Democratic two-party shares above the range of 5,000 simulated plans (p.8, Fig. 2). Partisan metrics depend on the statewide elections available in each state, so cross-state comparisons are not valid (p.5, p.8).
bearings.paper_location: p.5-8, Fig. 1-2; Measures section (ndshare, e_dvs, pr_dem)
bearings.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0 x exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0), where lean is one Cook PVI point oriented to the member's party. AL CA FL LA MO NC OH TN TX UT are FLAGGED as mid-decade redistricted, never altered. A separate flag fires when the 2025-to-2026 PVI shift is 5 or more points. Retirees take their 2025 seat PVI through ballot overrides. c carries no uncertainty term.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The ensembles cover 2020-cycle maps only. They do not include the 2025-26 mid-decade redraws that the system flags, and they describe counterfactual neutral maps, not the realized seat a member runs in. At most they could add a per-district map-sensitivity band or a cross-check of Cook lean against ndshare. Per the paper, ndshare is not comparable across states. Reciprocity and the c amplitude/scale stay unvalidated (D-104..D-108). This is not evidence for them.

bearings.paper_claim: VEST precinct returns are estimated down to 2010 blocks and crosswalked to 2020 blocks, then aggregated to any district plan. Each state's output is a redist_map object plus 5,000 plans: 1,000 precincts x 5 districts x 5,001 plans gives 25,005 rows (p.3-5).
bearings.system_side: The scraper pulls ACS 2024 1-year on 119th-Congress districts and CBP 2020 on 116th-Congress districts and stacks them. Some new districts come back NA. The boundary mismatch is documented but never quantified.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The block-crosswalk recipe could re-aggregate county or ZIP CBP counts onto 119th boundaries, but only with population-weighted allocation. That allocation adds its own error, because establishments are not distributed like population. The paper reports no estimate of that error, so it gives a method only, not an answer to the component's question about measurement error.

gaps_exposed: Competitiveness c treats Cook PVI as an exact point, with no band for uncertainty or map dependence. The 10 redistricted states are flagged but not adjusted, and no alternative lean source (for example ndshare from statewide elections) is cross-checked.
No ensemble or baseline exists for the 2025-26 mid-decade maps. Public 50-state ensembles stop at the 2020 cycle.
The census district metrics mix 119th-Congress ACS with 116th-Congress CBP boundaries. The resulting measurement error has never been estimated, and no crosswalk re-aggregation exists.
flags: Competing interests: C.T.K. was paid by the Maryland Redistricting Commission, and K.I. was a paid expert witness in Alabama, Kentucky, Ohio and South Carolina cases (p.10). Weigh the gerrymander-detection framing accordingly.
The paper is internally inconsistent: the abstract says simulated 2020 plans, while the Background says 2022 plans (p.1-2).

Do not quote any partisan statistic from this dataset across states. Per the paper, each state's partisan metrics rest on different statewide elections. Any figure must name its state, its election window and its 5,000-plan denominator.
No conflict with D-021, D-025 or the two rejected SNA proposals. The paper does not touch networks or LDA.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotated-bibliography entries or highlights for this work (n_annots 0), so there is no takeaway to compare and nothing is stale. The closest live system choice is Paul's 2026-10-05 ruling to flag, never alter, the mid-decade-redistricted states in the competitiveness build. The paper neither contradicts nor validates that ruling. Its ensembles predate those redraws.

related.why: Both use ensembles of algorithmically sampled districting plans as the neutral baseline for judging maps and criteria.
Best asks whether commissions avoid partisan gerrymanders. McCartan supplies the outlier-versus-ensemble benchmark such an evaluation needs.
DeLuca validates BISG race estimation for redistricting. McCartan's VRA constraint relies on district minority VAP shares, the measurement DeLuca's method addresses.
The SMC sampler and its convergence diagnostics (Gelman-Rubin R of about 1.05 or less, resampling weights) extend the basic Monte Carlo sampling that Harrison introduces.
